Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette:
The assault happened on a warm September night, just after her nineteenth birthday. Leila had been walking home from a friend’s apartment when a man emerged from the alley beside the shuttered laundromat. She remembered the smell of alcohol on his breath, thick and sour, before he grabbed her wrist and pulled her into the darkness. He shouted in Arabic—words she did not understand but whose cadence she would never forget—and then the motorcycle roared past, its engine drowning out her scream. She had not thought she could stop it. Somebody else would have, she later told herself, somebody braver or faster. She had frozen, and that failure became the story she told herself about who she now was.

In the weeks that followed, Leila found she could not control when the memory returned. A passing motorcycle on the street outside her apartment would bring it back without warning—the full sensory flood: the alcohol smell, the shouting, the vibration of the engine through her bones. Now, every street she had learned to avoid became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked to the grocery store was its own daily acknowledgement of the alley, the shouting, the man who had been there. She would hear the man’s voice in her head, the exact pitch and rhythm, as though he were still there. She began to avoid going out after dark, and she stopped looking at her own body in the mirror, because seeing the faint bruise that had long since faded made her feel the grip on her wrist again. She also avoided the date—September 14th—as though the calendar itself was a trap.

Her husband, Omar, worked the evening shift at a warehouse, and Leila spent her nights alone in their small apartment. She listened constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering: the creak of the hallway floorboards, the jingle of keys, the click of the lock. Every noise seemed intentional. She would get up three or four times to check the chain, and when she finally lay back down, the memory would surge again—the alley, the shouting, the smell—and she would be certain that she was no longer capable of the simple things that had once defined her: walking home, trusting a quiet street, feeling safe in her own skin. Without ever staying in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, without ever walking past the alley in daylight to see that it was just a passage between two buildings, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the night it was set. The more she checked, the more the memories intruded, and the more she believed that someone else would have handled it better, that she had been weak.

She began to look behind her constantly, even in daylight, even inside the grocery store. She told herself it was caution, but the checking fed something darker: each time she saw nothing, she felt relief, but the relief never lasted, and the next glance confirmed that danger was always possible. The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the looking, the constant vigilance — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better, that she was exactly as fragile and incapable as she feared. The world had become a place where a man could appear from nowhere, and her beliefs about how things worked—that people were basically good, that bad things happened to other people—had been destroyed. She started to hear the shouting in her head more often, triggered by nothing she could name, and then she would smell the alcohol again, and the cycle would tighten.

By the time winter came, Leila had not left the apartment after four in the afternoon for three months. She had stopped answering calls from her mother, who did not understand why her daughter had become so distant. Omar had started sleeping on the couch because she would wake him at 2 a.m. to check the door. She knew this was not normal, but she also knew that if she stopped listening, stopped checking, stopped avoiding, something terrible would happen. It was Omar who finally found a clinic number and handed it to her. She took it because she was exhausted, but what frightened her most was the thought that even therapy could not undo what she had become.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about weakness).
No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences triggers (e.g., makes cues more salient).
No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about weakness).
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences triggers (e.g., makes cues more salient).
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
